title: Gap Sensitivity and Bottleneck Migration in Sparse Constraint-Preserving Quantum Annealing
abstract: Constraint-preserving exchange drivers allow many coupling graphs that preserve the same feasible sector, but exhibit different minimum gaps along an annealing path. We derive an exchange-resolved sensitivity of the normalised minimum gap for fixed-cardinality Laplacian drivers sharing a Dicke ground state, and apply it to identify locally favourable modifications of the driver. Numerical experiments indicate this sensitivity reliably predicts beneficial infinitesimal changes, but its reliability decreases when the same direction is extended to a finite edge replacement. The gap landscape tracking reveals one mechanism of this loss of reliability. Improving the active bottleneck can expose a competing minimum, with a more extensive reorganisation of the low-energy subspace. We call this the "repair-and-expose" mechanism and observe it in both dense quadratic and sparse frustrated objective families. This motivates relinearizing the response when competing minima become co-active. In the tested oracle setting, a tied-minimum max-min update is substantially more reliable than continuing the original direction or optimizing only the incoming minimum. Supporting finite-size search and selector tests show that this local information can remain useful beyond the infinitesimal limit, while its practical extraction depends on the driver geometry and identification of the relevant low-energy competitors. These results connect local exchange-resolved gap sensitivity to bottleneck migration and conditional driver redirection.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how to optimize the minimum energy gap during quantum annealing by studying the 'exchange-resolved sensitivity' of the system's gap. It finds that while local changes are predictable, finite updates require accounting for 'bottleneck migration' via a 'repair-and-expose' mechanism. The results suggest that a max-min update rule is superior for guiding the annealing process when multiple low-energy states compete.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to design constraint-preserving drivers in quantum annealing to reliably improve the minimum gap ($\min_s \Delta(s, w)$) of the annealing path.
main_result: Local gap sensitivity reliably predicts beneficial infinitesimal changes, but finite edge replacements require a 'repair-and-expose' mechanism and a 'tied-minimum max-min update' for reliable continuation.
method: The analysis derives the exchange-resolved sensitivity of the minimum gap using Hellmann–Feynman theorems and compares local (infinitesimal) versus finite updates.
model_or_system: The model involves binary optimization problems with fixed-cardinality constraints, analyzed via an annealing path $H(s, w) = (1 -s)D(w) + sP$. The driver $D(w)$ is constructed from exchange Laplacians.
key_observables: Minimum Gap ($\Delta(s, w)$), Exchange-Resolved Sensitivity, Subspace Overlap ($O_{	ext{sub}}$), and the Dirichlet-energy contrast ($G_e(s)$).
important_parameters: The analysis distinguishes between infinitesimal changes ($\alpha \ll 1$) and finite edge replacements ($\alpha=1$), and uses various step sizes ($\epsilon=10^{-2}$ or $10^{-3}$).
main_assumptions: The local sensitivity analysis assumes simple eigenvalues and a unique minimizer $s^*$; the max-min rule is presented as a local continuation method.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the distinction between the physical exchange graph and the induced configuration-space swap graph; other figures compare gap improvements across different optimization strategies.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework for gap sensitivity, derives the local response, identifies the 'repair-and-expose' mechanism when bottlenecks migrate, and proposes the 'tied-minimum max-min update' rule for reliable driver redirection.
why_interesting: The focus on gap dynamics, bottleneck identification, and local optimization rules directly relates to understanding the energy landscape traversal in complex quantum many-body systems, which is central to condensed matter physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A physical exchange graph and its induced fixed-cardinality swap graph. Physical vertices represent binary variables, whereas configuration-space vertices represent feasible strings. A single physical edge generates all allowed configuration swaps across that variable pair.

FIG. 2. Oracle-selected directions from local perturbations to complete edge replacements. The 798 non-abstained starts each define one fixed replacement path S0 →S1 parameterized by α. All selected directions improve the re-minimized gap at α = 10−3 and 10−2, whereas the full replacement at α = 1 improves 662/798 = 82.96% of paths. Fractional α values are weighted diagnostic drivers outside the unit-weight B-edge class. Finite candidate gaps are not used to select the direction; the line connects the tested step sizes as a visual guide.

FIG. 3. Example of a resolved bottleneck exchange along one oracle-selected driver update. Two distinct local minima coex- ist and reverse their depth ordering as α increases. In the illus- trated B = 6 path, their gaps become equal near α = 0.144959, at annealing locations s ≃0.337921 and 0.436638. The original bottleneck is first raised, after which the competing minimum becomes globally limiting. Both branches increase in the dis- played neighborhood; the incoming branch becomes limiting because it increases more slowly. This “repair-and-expose” behavior is the finite-update mechanism examined in the text; cohort-level statistics use all 798 non-abstained paths.

FIG. 4. Initial-to-final low-energy subspace overlap, evaluated at each driver’s active minimum, for 377 paths without a resolved switch and 421 switching paths. The medians are 0.915 and 0.449, respectively. The path groups share the same 30 objectives, so their separation is an association rather than an independent-sample causal comparison. Both the driver and the active annealing coordinate change in this diagnostic. All 798 comparisons satisfy E2 −E1 > 10−9 at both evaluation points; no rank-two comparison was excluded.

FIG. 5. Refined-minimum basin-pair diagnostic pooled de- scriptively over nine cells of 30 accepted objectives, using the same conditioned ensemble as Table V and Appendix A 3. There are 152 matching pairs and 118 mismatches. The two rightmost groups contain the same 118 observations, first using the practical pair and then the retrospective crossing-relevant pair. Boxes show medians and interquartile ranges; whiskers use the standard 1.5-IQR convention and points show outliers. Negative Q values are allowed by Eq. (43). The retrospective pair is used only as a diagnostic reference and is not available to the practical selector.
